paras: The killing of William Stephens was the shooting of a Black farmer at his door near Pacio, Delta County, Texas, in August 1895 by "white caps," after he stayed past a ten-day notice ordering him to leave. Carried from Paris, Texas, on his mother's word, the killing was reported within a white-cap campaign that had driven Black residents from Delta County "almost to a man." The wire story that spread the news also quoted a local merchant who knew of no such killing.

One night in the week before Aug. 5, 1895, according to a Paris dispatch, every Black resident of Delta County was told to leave "or he would be taken out and hanged." The notices set off a flight that left some 2,000 acres abandoned, crops and all, while some Black owners of valuable farms stayed behind to sell. By Aug. 8 the movement had reached Lamar County, where the Black church at Glory was burned, and Delta County families had taken refuge in Paris.

On Aug. 12 an elderly Black woman named Stephens reached Paris from near Pacio and said her son had been called to the door about 4 o'clock Saturday morning and "shot down by the white caps." His ten-day notice had just expired, and he had not joined the exodus because his growing crops and home would have been put at risk. He left a wife and two children, and a brother living in Paris had fled when he first received a notice.

The San Francisco Call's dispatch added that he had tried to sell his crop but found no buyer, and that he was killed before his wife, mother and children. The two accounts placed the notice differently, near his house in the wire and on his door in the Call.

Officers were said to be pursuing the perpetrators, but no arrest, inquest or trial for the killing appears in the coverage. The same day a Paris afternoon paper printed an appeal from "the colored people of Delta county" asking Lamar County whites to protect them: "We are not guilty of the least crime in Delta county." A Paris evening paper urged officers to send the white caps to "the penitentiary or the gallows" and told citizens to arm themselves against them.

Legal action followed in Lamar County instead, where an inquest at Glory on Aug. 13 heard a confession naming a man said to have come from Delta County to organize the band. Two suspects in the church burning were jailed on Aug. 14, but the Call had no news that day from Delta County. On Aug. 23 a Paris special to the Fort Worth Gazette reported every Black resident gone from Delta County and a second man, Jeff Cole, "riddled with bullets" after a ten-day notice; it did not mention Stephens.

The Paris wire ran on Aug. 13 in the Salt Lake Herald, the Deseret Evening News, the Indianapolis Journal, the Providence News and the Maysville Evening Bulletin. Headlines ranged from the Indianapolis Journal's "SHOT BY WHITE CAPS" to the Maysville paper's "WHITE CAP CARNIVAL" and the Providence News's "THE NEGROES APPEAL." The wire attributed the account to the mother, said the white caps were "alleged to be holding carnival," and ended on "Reports are conflicting."

The New York Sun gave the case a single flat sentence in a column of crimes, calling Stevens "a thrifty negro farmer" who was "shot dead." The Call ran its own dispatch under "WORK OF THE WHITE CAPS," calling the band "outlaws" whose lawlessness was "not countenanced by the whites generally." A Michigan weekly summed the affair up in two sentences on Aug. 24; the one Texas paper found, the Fort Worth Gazette, reported only the later Cole killing, and no Black-press coverage was found.

Joe Price, a merchant living several miles from the scene, said that so far as he knew no Black man had been shot or murdered by white caps. The date also differs: the mother placed the shooting on Saturday morning, Aug. 10, while the Sun's Aug. 12 dispatch said "last night." The name was printed as Stephens, Stevens and Stephen.

reader.title: Killing of William Stephens
bases: A band called 'white caps' posted ten-day notices ordering Black residents out of Delta County and shot Stephens at his door after his notice expired (A1, A5, A6).

The papers report Stephens shot dead without any legal process by 'the white caps' for staying past an order to leave, a racial pretext (A5, A6, A3); the number of men at his door is not given, and a Paris merchant said he knew of no such killing (A5).

The killing rests on the mother's account carried in two separate Paris dispatches (A5, A6) and a brief (A3), while the same wire quoted merchant Joe Price saying he knew of no Black man shot by white caps and that 'Reports are conflicting' (A5, A4).

framing.detail: The Paris wire ran under headlines such as 'SHOT BY WHITE CAPS', 'WHITE CAP CARNIVAL' and 'THE NEGROES APPEAL', attributing the killing to the mother and closing on 'Reports are conflicting.'
The Call headed it 'WORK OF THE WHITE CAPS' and a 'Reign of Terror', called the perpetrators 'outlaws', and quoted a Paris editorial calling for 'the penitentiary or the gallows'.
The New York Sun gave the killing one flat sentence in a column of crimes, describing Stevens as 'a thrifty negro farmer'.
